---
title: "The product rule"
---

Suppose a corpus annotation establishes that half of the represented pronouns are plural and that eighty percent of the plural pronouns are accusative. The product rule recovers the joint probability that a pronoun is both plural and accusative from these two quantities.

The [definition of conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd) already contains the answer:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)}{\mathbb{P}(P)}.
$$

Here $P$ is the plural event and $A$ is the accusative event. Multiply both sides by $\mathbb{P}(P)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)
=\mathbb{P}(A\cap P).
$$

Writing the joint probability first gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
=\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P).
$$

This expression is the [**product rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html), also called the [**multiplication rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). It writes one joint probability as a product of a conditional probability and the probability of its condition.

## Reconstructing the joint probability

The pronoun measure gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(P)=.50
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.
$$

Substitute these two values into the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
&=\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)\\
&=.80\times.50\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The conditioning event $P$ receives half of the total probability, and $A$ receives eighty percent of the probability within $P$. Eighty percent of one half is $.40$.

We can check the same logic with counts. Imagine 100 pronoun tokens.

1. If 50 are plural, then the plural event contains 50 tokens.
2. If 80 percent of those 50 are accusative, then 40 tokens are both plural and accusative.
3. Those 40 tokens make up 40 percent of all 100 tokens.

The product rule expresses the same calculation in probabilities rather than counts.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_plural <- .50
p_acc_given_plural <- .80

p_plural_and_acc <- p_acc_given_plural * p_plural
p_plural_and_acc
```

The result is `.4`.

## The reverse factorization

An intersection is symmetric:

$$
A\cap P=P\cap A.
$$

We can thus begin from the opposite conditional probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

In the toy measure,

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)=\frac{.40}{.70}
$$

and $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$. The reversed product is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\times.70\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The factors differ because the conditioning event differs, but both products equal the probability of the same intersection.

This gives the identity

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)
=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

The [next page](bayes-rule.qmd) uses this equality to derive Bayes' rule. No additional probability assumption is needed.

## Factorization and dependence

The product rule is an algebraic rewriting of a joint probability and does not assert that $A$ and $P$ are independent. The factor $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)$ explicitly allows the probability of $A$ to depend on whether $P$ occurred.

For instance, suppose a speaker's use of a reduced form depends on whether the word is predictable in context. We can still factor the joint event as

$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{reduced}\cap\text{predictable})
=\mathbb{P}(\text{reduced}\mid\text{predictable})
 \mathbb{P}(\text{predictable}).
$$

The dependence appears in the conditional term. The multiplication sign does not justify replacing

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

That substitution requires [independence](independence.qmd), whereas the product rule holds whenever the conditional probability is defined.

## Check your understanding

1. Starting from the definition of $\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)$, derive $\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)$.
2. Suppose $\mathbb{P}(P)=.30$ and $\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.60$. Compute $\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)$ and interpret the result among 100 tokens.
3. Explain why the two orders of the product rule have different factors but the same product.
4. Which unjustified substitution treats the two chain rule factors as independent?

The two factorizations reconstruct the same intersection. On the [next page](bayes-rule.qmd), we equate them and solve for a reversed conditional probability.
